problems.title: Value-based padding deletes a real zero neighbor
problems.source_location: Eq.(4), PDF p.4; methods/lava.py, LAVA.forward, lines 13–21; dataset_augmented.py, slack projection
claim: LAVA sums truncated adjacent-vertex objective gaps. The release treats an all-zero projected vertex as padding.
analysis: Consider minimization on \(0\leq x\leq1\), represented by \(x+s=1\), with true cost \(-x\). The true optimum is \((1,0)\), whose genuine neighbor \((0,1)\) projects to \(x=0\) after slack removal. Predicted cost \(\hat c=1\) selects \(x=0\) with true regret \(1\). The real neighbor gap is \(1\), but the value-based padding test deletes it, yielding zero loss and zero gradient. Separately, mapping gaps below \(-\varepsilon\) to zero differs from the printed clamp: for \(\varepsilon=1/10\), gaps \(-1/5,-1/20\) violate scalar convexity since the midpoint maps to \(0>-1/40\). Their ordinary derivatives nevertheless agree away from the threshold.
result: The zero-neighbor mask changes the defined surrogate and its gradients on an allowed projected LP. The threshold-to-zero scalar difference alone does not establish different updates away from the kink. Proposition 4.1 remains intact.
repair: Carry an explicit neighbor-validity mask or count independent of coordinates, and clamp real gaps at \(-\varepsilon\) to match Eq.(4).
problems.impact_rationale: A valid zero-valued projected neighbor is deleted by the released mask, without evidence that this occurred in the benchmark arrays.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Integer-solution cache and filtering corrupt relaxed neighborhoods
claim: The knapsack workflow trains against relaxed optima, but caches neighbors by the integer optimum and removes neighbors equal to that integer solution.
analysis: For \(3x+2y\leq4\), \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), use costs \((4,3)\) then \((5,3)\). Both integer optima are \(I=(1,0)\); relaxed optima are respectively \(A=(2/3,1)\) and \(B=(1,1/2)\). Their neighbor sets are \(N(A)=\{B,(0,1)\}\) and \(N(B)=\{I,A\}\). Reusing the cache under key \(I\) supplies stale neighbors at \(B\). With predicted maximization cost \(q=(-1,-3)\), stale gaps are \(0,-1/2\), so the release returns no update, while the omitted actual neighbor \(I\) has gap \(3/2\). Even without a cache collision, filtering by the integer solution deletes \(I\). The selected integer decision is the origin, with true regret \(5\) under the second cost.
result: Both data-flow defects are concrete for the supported knapsack/relaxation interface. Their occurrence and effect in the original benchmark arrays are not established.
repair: Key by the actual relaxed vertex and constraint identity, or disable caching. Remove a self-neighbor only against that same relaxed label; retain all genuine adjacent vertices.
problems.impact_rationale: The release can use the wrong relaxed neighborhood, but the central adjacent-vertex theorem remains correct and benchmark impact is unknown.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Training-time accumulator excludes most training work
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF pp.7–8; utils/train_model.py, lines 43–44 and 66–103
claim: The paper describes training time including adjacent-vertex precomputation and actual training, excluding validation, and uses a \(600\)-second budget. The release times only the loss evaluation.
analysis: The prediction the regressor forward call precedes the timer; elapsed time is added before zero_grad, backward and optimizer.step. Hence an iteration records approximately \(t_{\rm loss}\), rather than \(t_{\rm pred}+t_{\rm loss}+t_{\rm back}+t_{\rm opt}\). These omitted operations are training, not validation. Precomputation is separately included.
result: The release timing definition does not match the stated protocol. It cannot recover a corrected speedup or establish that the archived commit generated the published plots.
repair: Time the complete prediction, loss, backward and optimizer step with a monotonic clock; add precomputation and consistently exclude validation. Remeasure the affected runtime comparisons if this path generated them.
problems.impact_rationale: The released timer omits training operations, but corrected speedups and correspondence to the published run have not been established.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Zero-margin optimality leaves solver ties unresolved
problems.source_location: Proposition 4.1 and sentence preceding Eq.(4), PDF p.4
claim: Making a labeled vertex predicted-cost optimal is described as giving zero regret, whereas the regret evaluates one selected optimizer.
analysis: For the unit square with true cost \((1,1)\), true optimum \((0,0)\), and nonzero predicted cost \((1,0)\), both \((0,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are predicted optima. The adjacent-vertex zero-margin loss is zero, but a solver may choose \((0,1)\), with true regret \(1\). Positive strict adjacent margins instead give a unique optimum, and the experiments use \(\varepsilon=0.1\).
result: This is a tie-handling qualification of a zero-margin interpretation, not a refutation of Proposition 4.1 or the positive-margin method. Tie-independent zero regret requires every predicted optimizer to be a true optimizer.
problems.impact_rationale: The adjacent-vertex theorem is correct; the zero-margin tie qualification does not refute the positive-margin method.
problems.existing_correction_status: No applicable author correction was established in this inspection.
